claim_mappings.value: After a hundred-year war Mahiṣa wins Indra’s office and divine jurisdictions; displaced gods roam earth. Led by Brahmā, they tell Śiva and Viṣṇu their defeat and seek a plan to kill him.
Displaced gods seek deliverance.

Divine energies converge as Devī: Śiva’s face, Yama’s hair, Viṣṇu’s arms, Moon’s breasts, Indra’s waist, Varuṇa’s legs/thighs, Earth’s hips, Brahmā’s feet, Sun’s toes, Vasus’ fingers, Kubera’s nose, Prajāpati’s teeth, Agni’s eyes, twilights’ brows and wind’s ears.
Gods’ energies manifest as a woman.

Śiva gives a trident; Viṣṇu a discus; Varuṇa a conch and noose; Agni a spear; wind a bow and full quivers; Indra a vajra and Airāvata’s bell; Yama a rod; Prajāpati a rosary; Brahmā a water-pot; Sun rays; Kāla sword and shield.
Devī receives divine equipment.

Milk Ocean supplies pearl necklace and imperishable garments; ornaments adorn Devī. Viśvakarman gives axe, diverse weapons and impenetrable armor; Ocean lotus garlands and lotus; Himavat lion and gems; Kubera a wine cup; Śeṣa a jeweled serpent necklace.
Devī is adorned and mounted.

Devī’s roar shakes worlds, sea, earth and mountains; gods and sages praise her. Mahiṣa musters armies and approaches its source. Her light, crown, bow sound and thousand arms fill the worlds; Cikṣura and Cāmara enter battle.
The battle begins.

Udagra, Mahāhanu, Asiloman, Bāṣkala, Biḍāla and huge contingents fight with missile and close weapons; Pargiter inserts Ugradarśana from Bombay’s reading where the displayed Sanskrit has no proper name. Mahiṣa leads enormous chariot, elephant and horse forces.
Named and collective contingents engage.

Devī cuts enemy missiles effortlessly. Her lion attacks; her breaths create energized troops carrying axes, javelins, swords and halberds, with drums and conchs. Her weapons kill and bind enemies; bell sound confounds them.
Devī’s breath-born army joins combat.

Mutilated demons and armed headless bodies continue fighting or dance to martial music. Fallen forces obstruct the field and blood forms rivers. Devī, lion and emanated troops destroy the host; gods shower flowers.
Mahiṣa’s army is destroyed.

Cikṣura shoots arrows; Devī cuts them, kills horses and driver, breaks bow and banner and wounds him. His sword strikes lion and Devī’s arm, then breaks. His thrown śūla and his body are shattered by hers.
Cikṣura is slain.

Elephant-mounted Cāmara hurls a spear; Devī’s huṃ renders it powerless, and arrows cut his next śūla. Lion leaps onto elephant, wrestles Cāmara on the ground, then springs and severs his head with a paw-blow.
Cāmara is slain.

Devī kills Udagra with stones/trees, Karāla with bodily blows, Uddhata with club, Bāṣkala with bhindipāla, Tāmra/Andhaka with arrows, Ugrāsya/Ugravīrya/Mahāhanu with trident, Biḍāla with sword and Durdhara/Durmukha with arrows.
Named chiefs are slain.
Buffalo-shaped Mahiṣa attacks troops with muzzle, hooves, tail, horns, rush, roar, circling and breath, then attacks lion. His movements shake earth, sea, clouds and mountains.
Mahiṣa confronts Devī directly.
Devī binds Mahiṣa. He changes buffalo to lion, then armed man as she cuts at him; arrows strike man, sword and shield. Elephant-form seizes lion; she cuts its trunk. He becomes buffalo again.
Mahiṣa’s successive forms are countered.

Devī drinks and laughs; arrows break hurled mountains. She tells Mahiṣa his roaring is brief, leaps, presses his neck and strikes with śūla. As he emerges halfway from the buffalo mouth, she beheads him. Gods rejoice; celestial singers and dancers celebrate.
Mahiṣāsura is slain.

Gods praise Devī’s cosmic power, knowledge, prosperity, protection and mercy in battle, including the claim that slain enemies reach heaven. They ask her gentle and fearsome forms and her weapons to protect every direction.
Gods worship the victorious Devī.

Gods offer flowers, perfumes and incense. Invited to choose a boon, they ask relief whenever they remember her in calamity and prosperity for mortals singing this hymn. She agrees and disappears; Medhas introduces her later emergence from Gaurī.
Devī grants remembrance-based protection.

adaptation_boundaries.rule: Every critical factual claim must cite evidence or be explicitly classified as adaptation.
Missing motivation, iconography, dialogue, chronology, or causality must not be invented.
A COMPLETE spine covers only its declared bounded chronology.

bounded_completeness.basis: All narrative scenes and conversations within this bounded arc read and source-order transitions recorded. COMPLETE denotes bounded narrative chronology, not every atomic hymn epithet or exhaustive chapter graph.

variants_and_conflicts.description: Pargiter main text Aruṇākṣa; its footnote gives Bombay Aruṇākhya. SanskritDocuments DM 11.52 reads Aruṇākhya, meaning named Aruṇa.
Wisdomlib index prose labels DM as chapters 82–92; actual linked chapter heading and narrative boundaries are 81–93. Catalogue uses linked headings.
DM9.30 calls Niśumbha ditija; record textual Diti-descendant descriptor, not an independently narrated biological mother–son genealogy.
Wisdomlib Pargiter display has corrupted rain/failure text and says heavy rain in the nourishment sentence; Sanskrit DM 11.46–48 explicitly says drought and nourishment until rain.
Sanskrit DM 11.50 explicitly announces Durgādevī after Durgama’s killing; the displayed Pargiter paragraph omits the name-sentence.
Pargiter canto 83 footnote 2 reports Bombay additions killing Kāla, Ugradarśana and Asiloman. These are footnote-attested variants, excluded from main event order pending edition inspection.
Pargiter’s killing sentence says heads and buttocks; Sanskrit has jaghane. Conventional thigh-position is not imposed until another reliable witness is inspected.
Pārvatī becoming Kālikā in ch5 and Kālī emanating from Ambikā in ch7 are separate source-scoped manifestation nodes; sameness not established by those scenes alone.
Pargiter interprets Kolāvidhvaṃsin as non-destroyers of Kolas; other common retellings translate destroyers. No etymological conclusion imposed.
Pargiter has Mauryas; SanskritDocuments DM 8.6 has Maurvas. Manuscript/print collation needed before standardizing the group-name.
Pargiter ch10 translates absorption into breasts; Sanskrit 10.6 says tanau, body. Graph records only absorption into Devī.
Ch8 emits Caṇḍikā’s Śakti named Śivadūtī; Pargiter ch9 note identifies Śivadūtī with Caṇḍikā. Main graph retains emanation, avoids silently collapsing entities.
Pargiter adopts Ugradarśana as a name from Bombay reading; SanskritDocuments DM 2.43–44 has a participle and no such proper name.
